meta-new-mexico-fine.headline: Meta hit with $567m New Mexico fine as child-safety penalties near $1bn
meta-new-mexico-fine.body_md:
Meta's legal bill for failing to protect children on Facebook and Instagram has climbed toward $1 billion in less than five months — and for the first time, a court isn't just making the company pay. It's making the company change its product.

A judge in Santa Fe, New Mexico, ordered Meta on August 7 to pay $567 million into a state fund for treating and preventing harm to young people, on top of the $375 million a jury already assessed against the company in March. Combined, the two penalties from a single case now total $942 million — and they come bundled with a set of court-mandated changes to how Instagram and Facebook work for anyone under 18.

![Entrance sign at Meta's headquarters complex in Menlo Park, California](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/43/Meta_Headquarters_Sign.jpg)

## A factory that pollutes

Judge Bryan Biedscheid, who oversaw the case after New Mexico's jury verdict, didn't reach for the language courts usually use for consumer-protection violations. He reached for an environmental-law metaphor instead.

> "The Court considers Meta's platforms to be analogous to the factory, the advertising and other content displayed on those platforms to be what is produced by the factory, and the psychological harm to and sexual exploitation of children to be the pollution that must be abated."

He went further, writing that "just as noxious pollution produced by the factory can harm the common public right to reasonably clean air, the harmful effects of Meta's platforms on children do not stay contained by its platforms" — they "migrate to the internet as a whole and, perhaps most concerning, to the real world."

That framing matters legally as much as rhetorically. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez sued Meta under public-nuisance law, the same legal theory historically used against polluters, opioid manufacturers and gun makers — not the theory typically used against a social network. A jury sided with the state in March, finding Meta had violated consumer-protection law by designing products that hook young users while concealing what it knew about child sexual exploitation happening on its platforms. Biedscheid's abatement order this month decides what the company now has to do about it.

## What actually changes for teenagers

The remedies go beyond a check-writing exercise. Under the order, Meta must, for users it identifies as under 18 in New Mexico:

- Hide like counts by default, restorable only with parental or guardian approval
- Pause push notifications overnight (10 p.m. to 7 a.m.) and during school hours on academic-year weekdays
- Cap combined Facebook and Instagram usage at roughly 90 hours a month — about three hours a day
- Make Instagram accounts private by default and unsearchable except by username
- Block adults from messaging minors they haven't previously connected with
- Build a dedicated model to predict under-13 users within two years, request age verification from suspected under-13 accounts, and delete data collected on children found to be under 13

Meta must also file compliance reports twice a year and set up an appeals process for users who believe the company misjudged their age. WhatsApp is exempt.

![Instagram app icon on a smartphone screen](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/49/Instagram_app_icon_on_smartphone_screen_%28perspective_render%29_%2849897226292%29.jpg)

$420 million of the new fund is earmarked for treatment services for young people harmed by the platforms; the rest goes to prevention, screening and awareness programs over five years, according to the New Mexico Department of Justice.

## Rounding error, precedent-setter

Set against Meta's finances, the number is almost trivial: the company reported roughly $60 billion in profit in 2025, making $942 million a fraction of a single quarter's earnings. Meta's stock barely moved, closing down less than half a percent at $589.44 on the day of the ruling. A company spokesperson said Meta "disagrees with the ruling and will appeal," adding that it has been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors from its platforms.

What's harder to shrug off is the template. More than 40 states and over 1,300 school districts have filed similar public-nuisance suits against social media companies, and Massachusetts' attorney general has already cleared a court hurdle to pursue Meta on nearly identical grounds. If other judges adopt Biedscheid's factory framing — treating engagement features as the product and psychological harm as an externality to be abated rather than merely penalized — the exposure stops being about fines altogether and starts being about which features companies are legally allowed to ship to minors.

That's the shift traders should note even if the dollar figure looks like noise: like counts, overnight notifications and open-ended scrolling are not incidental to the business model, they're tuned to maximize time-on-platform. A court ordering their removal for a chunk of the user base is a different kind of risk than a fine — one that scales with however many other states decide to follow New Mexico's lead.

Meta's appeal will test whether the remedy survives on review, likely stretching into 2027. Watch for how Massachusetts' case — already cleared to proceed after an April ruling — handles the same public-nuisance theory, and whether other state attorneys general cite Biedscheid's order directly in filings of their own.

colombia-earthquake-toll.headline: Colombia earthquake death toll passes 250 as rescuers search for survivors
colombia-earthquake-toll.body_md:
The earthquake gave Cali and Pereira almost no warning. At 7:34am on Monday, as commuters were pouring coffee and opening shop shutters, the ground beneath Colombia's Pacific coast and central Andes convulsed for nearly two minutes. By Tuesday morning the death toll stood at 254, with Pereira — 101 dead — and Cali — 95 dead — bearing the worst of it. As of Wednesday, search teams were still working through collapsed buildings in four cities, and the toll was continuing to rise.

The US Geological Survey put the magnitude at 7.4, with an epicentre some 20 kilometres from San José del Palmar in Chocó department and a depth of 110 kilometres — deep enough that the shaking radiated outward across a wide swathe of the country rather than concentrating destruction narrowly. Colombia's national geological service called it the strongest quake to hit the country so far this century, eclipsing anything recorded since a magnitude-7.2 event struck near Tumaco in 1979. Tremors reached Bogotá, 400 kilometres east, and were felt as far as Ecuador and Panama.

![Cali, Colombia's third-largest city, seen before Monday's earthquake](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Cali_downtown-_skyline.jpg/1280px-Cali_downtown-_skyline.jpg)

## A widening search

Gloria Giraldo, a 38-year-old housewife in one of the neighbourhoods that came down around her, put it plainly: "Since yesterday we've been wondering what will become of our lives." In Cali, 22-year-old journalism student Luis Saenz was drinking his morning coffee when the shaking started. "For me, the earthquake felt eternal," he said.

Official counts put more than 2,500 people injured and, by some tallies, over 4,000 still missing — a figure aid agencies caution will fall as communications are restored and rise as more bodies are recovered from rubble. Rescue workers have been listening for signs of life in the wreckage; near one collapsed building in Cali, volunteer Andrés Felipe Mejía described a rescuer asking anyone trapped to whistle. "Someone whistled back," he said. Aid groups regard the 48-to-72-hour window after a quake as the most critical for finding survivors — a window that, five days on, has largely closed, shifting the operation from rescue toward recovery.

The destruction is concentrated in the cities strung along Colombia's central mountain corridor. In Cali, the country's third-largest city, more than 5,000 buildings were damaged and at least 40 collapsed, among them three floors of the Hospital Universitario del Valle, forcing the evacuation of over 600 patients. Pereira lost part of its airport terminal and dozens of structures, including a law-school building at Universidad Libre. In Manizales, a tower of the city's basilica cathedral came down. President Abelardo de la Espriella, touring the wreckage, said it "broke my heart going through the city centre and seeing all these businesses destroyed." He has declared a state of national disaster and deployed more than 1,000 soldiers, while offers of help have arrived from Ecuador, the United States — which pledged $15.5 million — El Salvador, Venezuela, Mexico and half a dozen other governments.

## The coffee axis goes quiet

![Coffee plantations in Colombia's central growing region](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Cafetales%2C_en_Colombia.jpg/1280px-Cafetales%2C_en_Colombia.jpg)

The geography of the disaster is what gives it a second life beyond the humanitarian story. Pereira and Manizales sit at the heart of Colombia's so-called coffee axis — the departments of Caldas, Risaralda and Quindío that together grow roughly a quarter of the country's arabica crop. Colombia is the world's second-largest producer of premium arabica beans, behind only Brazil, and the quake struck during a period when global stockpiles certified for delivery on the ICE exchange were already thin.

The more immediate problem for exporters is logistics rather than lost trees. Maersk said terminal operations at Buenaventura — the Pacific port that handles the bulk of Colombia's coffee shipments — were temporarily suspended, and Bloomberg reported that exports were largely paused as landslides and debris closed key highways linking the growing region to the coast. Arabica futures in New York whipsawed on the news, touching a three-week high before giving back some of the gain as traders weighed a disrupted supply chain against production that, so far, appears structurally intact.

Oil and gas infrastructure, by contrast, seems to have been spared the worst. Ecopetrol's refineries at Barrancabermeja and Cartagena continued operating, and the pipeline network feeding the Coveñas export terminal on the Caribbean coast reported no interruption — a reminder that Colombia's energy infrastructure sits mostly outside the earthquake zone, even as its agricultural heartland does not.

## An economy on emergency footing

Colombia's government moved this week to declare an economic emergency, a legal mechanism that would let de la Espriella issue tax and spending decrees without waiting on Congress. Finance Minister Miguel Gómez told lawmakers the declaration could come within days, framing the moment as "the worst economic crisis in Colombian history" while pledging not to raise taxes to pay for reconstruction. Perhaps counterintuitively, the peso has firmed for five consecutive trading sessions since the quake — a sign, for now, that currency markets are pricing the disaster as a fiscal and humanitarian shock rather than a threat to the country's export earnings.

Whether that calm holds depends on what happens at Buenaventura in the coming days. If the port and the mountain highways reopen quickly, this becomes a short, sharp disruption that coffee traders absorb within weeks. If roadblocks persist through the September harvest window, the story shifts from rescue to supply, and arabica prices — already sensitive to any hint of tightness — become the mechanism by which the earthquake is felt far beyond Colombia's coffee axis.

uk-organoids-animal-testing.headline: UK scientists to grow mini human organs from NHS patient cells to cut animal testing
uk-organoids-animal-testing.body_md:
A mouse, no matter how carefully bred, cannot tell a researcher which drug will work in a particular patient's gut, liver or brain. That mismatch — between the animal in the cage and the human in the clinic — is the reason more than 90% of drugs that clear animal trials still fail when they reach people. It is also the reason Cambridge and Oxford are now racing to grow tiny, working versions of human organs from NHS patients' own tissue.

The Cambridge effort is anchored by a new £20m research hub funded by the Medical Research Council, based at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute. Its job is not just to grow organoids — clusters of cells, sometimes just a few millimetres across, that replicate the architecture and function of a real organ — but to standardise them into a library that academic labs and pharmaceutical companies can actually use. That distinction matters. Organoid science has existed for over a decade; what has been missing is a version reliable enough for industry to bet a drug programme on.

![Kidney organoids grown from human stem cells, imaged in test chambers](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3f/Kidney_Organoids_%2846580296595%29.jpg)

## A library of guts, tumours and brains

Matthias Zilbauer, a clinical professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute, put the logic bluntly: "A mouse cannot tell us what treatments work," he said, adding that the hub should have "a major impact on the numbers of animals used." Teams are starting with organoids modelling inflammatory bowel disease — ulcerative colitis and Crohn's — because those conditions vary enormously between patients and animal models have historically been poor predictors of which drug helps which person. Other groups are growing tumour organoids, or "tumoroids," to test cancer drugs against a patient's own cancer before it is given to them, work pioneered at Cambridge by Meritxell Huch. Further down the pipeline sit beating heart tissue and electrically active brain organoids for neurological disease.

![Intestinal organoid grown from Lgr5+ stem cells, imaged under a microscope](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a0/Intestinal_organoid.PNG)

A smaller, commercial strand of the same push comes from VivoSphere, whose chief technology officer Yuan Tian described the appeal to drug developers in risk terms: when a candidate compound fails on human tissue in a dish, "lower risk for animals and patients" follows, because it never proceeds to the next, more expensive and more ethically fraught stage of testing.

## Oxford's parallel bet

Oxford is building its own version. The Oxford Organoid Hub, housed in the university's Sherrington Building and co-directed by Christopher Toepfer and Filipa Simões, is assembling a patient-derived stem cell biobank linked to real clinical data and outcomes — the idea being that an organoid is only as useful as the medical history attached to the tissue it came from. Where Cambridge's hub leans toward gut and liver disease, Oxford's is being built to support multi-organ systems that model how organs interact, which matters for testing drug safety as much as efficacy.

Neither project claims organoids can fully replace animals yet. A government-commissioned review in February found "a gap in maturity of in vitro pre-clinical models developed in academic settings compared to the translational readiness required for a model to be used in industry" — polite science-speak for: promising in a university lab, not yet proven enough for a regulator to sign off a drug on that evidence alone. Many organoids still lack blood vessels, capping how large and realistic they can grow, and they miss immune cells that shape how a real organ responds to a drug.

## The numbers behind the push

The UK used 2.54 million animals in scientific procedures in 2025, a 3.8% fall on the year before and the lowest total since the law governing animal research took effect in 1987. Mice and rats still account for 95% of that figure. In November, science minister Lord Vallance set out a roadmap to accelerate the decline further: animal testing for skin and eye irritation is due to be phased out by the end of this year, with mouse-based botulinum toxin testing following in 2027. That roadmap carries £60m to help alternative methods clear the regulatory bar, on top of £15.9m from the Medical Research Council, Innovate UK and Wellcome for human tissue models, and a separate £2m from Innovate UK specifically aimed at cutting the use of dogs and monkeys in safety testing. The US Food and Drug Administration announced a parallel shift last year, saying animal testing should become "the exception rather than the norm" for monoclonal antibody safety data within three to five years.

![A laboratory mouse](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f4/Lab_mouse_mg_3158.jpg)

## What this threatens — and what it doesn't yet

The economic stakes are large enough to explain why both universities and government are moving now rather than waiting for the science to fully mature. Pharmaceutical companies collectively spend close to $300bn a year on research and development, and getting a single drug to market costs upward of $1.3bn once failures are priced in — failures that organoid advocates argue happen too late and too expensively under the current animal-testing-first model. The organoid market itself is forecast to grow at roughly 22% a year through 2030, reaching over $6.5bn, and industry estimates suggest organ-chip and organoid methods could save the sector several billion dollars annually simply by killing bad drug candidates earlier. That is also, implicitly, a threat to the contract research organisations that have built businesses around animal toxicology testing — several of the larger ones, aware of the direction of travel, are already investing in organoid platforms of their own rather than waiting to be undercut.

Dr Juliet Dukes of the charity Replacing Animals in Research called the approach one with "real potential to deliver truly personalised medicine" — a claim that is easier to make than to prove at scale. The honest state of play, per the February review, is that organoids work convincingly in individual academic papers but have not yet been standardised enough for a regulator or a pharma safety board to trust them wholesale. The next marker to watch is whether Cambridge's library produces organoid batches consistent enough for industry partners to actually adopt, rather than merely admire — a test that will start to be answered as the hub's first standardised models reach outside labs over the coming year.

gb-sprinters-european-100m.headline: GB's Glave and Azu claim European 100m one-two in Birmingham
gb-sprinters-european-100m.body_md:
Britain had come to Birmingham hoping for one medal in the men's 100 metres. It left with two of the top three, a national title reclaimed, and a story about redemption that Romell Glave had been waiting two years to tell.

Glave won the European 100m final in 10.09 seconds on Tuesday night, with fellow Briton Jeremiah Azu taking silver in 10.16. Germany's Owen Ansah completed the podium in 10.19. It was Britain's third British one-two in the event's history, following Darren Campbell's win over Dwain Chambers in 1998 and Zharnel Hughes's over Reece Prescod in 2018 — and it came at the expense of the defending champion, Italy's Marcell Jacobs, who pulled up injured halfway down the track and limped home in 12.26 seconds.

![Jeremiah Azu competing for Great Britain at the European Championships](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/aa/Jeremiah_Azu_%28GBR%29_2022.jpg)

## From bronze to gold

Two years ago in Rome, Glave stood on the same podium a step lower, watching Jacobs take European gold. "It's the redemption from the European Championships where I finished behind Jacobs," the 26-year-old said afterwards, framing Tuesday's win as unfinished business rather than a surprise. "Now is my time to dominate."

The Jamaica-born sprinter's route to a European title has not been a straight line. Once billed as the world's fastest 17-year-old after clocking 10.21 seconds in 2017, Glave spent much of his early twenties battling injuries before breaking the ten-second barrier for the first time in June this year. His personal best now stands at 9.97 seconds, set in London earlier this season.

Azu's silver was its own vindication. The Cardiff-raised sprinter, born in Rotterdam to a Ghanaian family, arrived in Birmingham as reigning world and European indoor 60m champion but without a global outdoor 100m medal to his name. That gap closed on Tuesday, adding to the Olympic bronze he won as part of Britain's 4x100m relay squad in Paris two years ago.

## A short race, a long story

The drama, inevitably, attached itself to Jacobs. The Italian had run the fastest time of the semi-finals at 10.08 seconds, arriving in the final as the man to beat before pulling up with what appeared to be a muscular injury in the race's opening third. His limp finish left the field to sort itself out among the rest, and Britain's strength in depth did the rest — Glave and Azu were two of three Britons in the field.

For a domestic athletics correspondent, a British one-two on home soil is as good as this beat gets: a strong squad, a settling of old scores, and a data point — 10.09 and 10.16 — that suggests genuine strength heading into next year's global season rather than a one-off. There is no broader read-through here; sprinting results of this kind move television audiences and column inches, not markets.

Attention now turns to the World Athletics Championships next year, where Glave and Azu will hope to convert continental form into a first global outdoor medal apiece — assuming Jacobs, too, returns fit enough to reclaim his spot at the sharp end of the field.

uk-europe-solar-eclipse.headline: UK and Europe brace for deepest solar eclipse since 1999
uk-europe-solar-eclipse.body_md:
There is a particular kind of quiet that falls over a solar farm during an eclipse — panels that were humming along at full tilt an hour earlier suddenly delivering a fraction of the current, then clawing it back just as fast once the Moon slides clear. This evening, that quiet arrives across an entire continent at once.

A total solar eclipse cuts a path from Siberia across the Arctic, over Greenland, and down through western Iceland before curving into northern Spain — Reykjavík, A Coruña, Oviedo, Bilbao, Valencia — and out towards the Balearic Islands, with up to two minutes eighteen seconds of totality visible from Iceland. It is the first total eclipse to touch mainland Europe since 11 August 1999, when the shadow last crossed Cornwall and northern France. Twenty-seven years is a long wait, though Europe won't have to wait as long again: a second total eclipse crosses southern Spain and Gibraltar next August, before the path goes quiet until 2081.

The UK misses totality — that won't return to British shores until 2090 — but it gets close. The Royal Observatory Greenwich puts coverage at around 82% in Edinburgh and Glasgow, rising to 90% over London, Bristol and Cardiff, and reaching roughly 95% in Cornwall, with the Isles of Scilly seeing as much as 96.5% of the Sun blotted out. First contact in London comes at 6:17pm, maximum eclipse at 7:12pm, and the Moon clears the Sun by around 8:06pm — a window that, conveniently for grid engineers, falls as the evening sun is already sliding towards the horizon.

## A stress test with 27 years' notice

For astronomers this is spectacle; for the people who keep Europe's lights on, it is a scheduled drill. The National Energy System Operator expects Great Britain to lose around 700 megawatts of solar generation at the eclipse's peak, with historical modelling suggesting the figure could run as high as 1.3 gigawatts — enough, NESO says, to power roughly half a million homes — against a maximum ramp rate approaching 4,400 MW an hour as output first collapses and then rebounds. Across the wider European grid, transmission body ENTSO-E has pencilled in a dip of up to 9.7 gigawatts of photovoltaic capacity, a number that has grid operators from Germany to the Netherlands lining up gas-fired backup capacity to smooth the swing.

Unlike a total blackout of demand, an eclipse announces its arrival to the minute, years in advance, which is precisely why operators treat it less as a threat than as a rehearsal for the faster, less predictable ramps that cloud cover throws at increasingly solar-heavy grids. The timing helps too: because the eclipse falls in early evening rather than at midday, when panels are already easing off for the day, the shortfall is gentler than the raw wattage figures suggest.

Octopus Energy is leaning into the moment rather than just absorbing it, offering customers who dial down consumption during the eclipse window up to 16 kWh of free electricity through its rewards scheme. "When the sun goes off grid," the supplier told customers, "we want you to do the same." Whether enough households take up the offer to matter is beside the point — it is a small, cheerful piece of demand-side flexibility dressed up as a sky-watching event.

The next comparable test comes on 2 August 2027, when totality returns to southern Spain and Gibraltar. Between now and then, the more immediate marker is simpler: whether NESO's ramp-rate forecasts hold up against what actually happens on Britain's grid this evening.

uk-heatwave-cobra-cost.headline: Burnham chairs Cobra as UK heatwave costs economy £4.4bn this year
uk-heatwave-cobra-cost.body_md:
Andy Burnham convened an emergency Cobra meeting on Wednesday, pulling in the Environment Agency, the Home Office, Defra and the Department of Health to confront a summer that has, by the government's own reckoning, moved from uncomfortable to unmanageable. Temperatures reached 33°C on the day of the meeting and were forecast to hit 38°C by Thursday, arriving on top of a wildfire season fire services describe as the worst on record and a drought now gripping most of England and Wales. It was the second such meeting this year — the first came in June, when a separate heat spike forced the same set of ministers into the same room.

What distinguishes this round is the arrival of a number. Analysis from the green thinktank Verdant put the cost of Britain's 2026 heatwaves at £4.4bn in lost economic output through July, up from an initial £2.36bn estimate for June alone. For a government that has spent the summer managing wildfires and standpipe logistics, that figure turns a weather story into a growth story — and gives the Treasury a line item it did not have before.

## A wildfire season without precedent

The scale is not in dispute. Fire services across England and Wales have tackled 966 wildfires so far in 2026, including 458 in July alone — already the busiest month on record — and a further 185 in the first ten days of August. A blaze that broke out near Ringwood in Hampshire, ignited by a vehicle fire on the A31, spread into New Forest heathland home to rare and protected species, one of several incidents straining crews this month.

![Firefighters tackle a heathland blaze during a UK heatwave](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/51/Fire_at_Shirley_Hills.jpg)

Steve Wright, general secretary of the Fire Brigades Union, described the situation as a "national emergency" already under way, arguing that crews "do not have the new modern equipment to deal with these" fires — a capacity complaint that sits awkwardly next to a government insisting it is responding with urgency. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper's public message was more cautious in tone, urging people simply to heed heat warnings, underscoring a gap between what the union says is needed on the ground and what ministers are offering by way of resource.

## Drought spreads faster than the response

Behind the fires sits a drier problem still. The Environment Agency now classifies 71.3% of England as in "flash drought" — conditions that developed rapidly on the back of the driest July on record — with almost three-quarters of the country affected once prolonged dry-weather zones are included. Seven of the agency's operational areas, from East Anglia to Devon and Cornwall, have moved into formal drought status. Roughly 45 million people live in the affected areas, more than 27 million are under water-use restrictions, and around 20 million are subject to hosepipe bans.

![A reservoir in England during a summer drought, with water levels far below capacity](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/64/Abberton_Run_Dry_-_geograph.org.uk_-_2534412.jpg)

The practical consequences reach beyond gardens. Farmers face restricted irrigation and, in places, early harvests on light land in the south and east, though this year's crop looks likely to be uneven rather catastrophic — reasonable yields on heavier, wetter soils offsetting real losses elsewhere. Downing Street has acknowledged as much: a spokesperson said the government understood that firefighters, farmers and NHS staff were all facing challenges connected to the weather, a rare instance of a government naming the stress across three separate frontline services in a single sentence.

## What Cobra actually buys

A Cobra meeting is coordination machinery, not policy in itself, and Wednesday's session produced no announced package — no emergency fund for fire services, no compensation scheme for farmers, no water infrastructure spending. That absence is where Verdant's economic analysis becomes more than background colour. The thinktank's research points to 30°C as a threshold beyond which labour productivity drops sharply, hitting construction and agriculture hardest because those sectors cannot simply move indoors. It is calling on the government to set a legal maximum working temperature and to be ready to compensate workers whose hours are cut by heat — recommendations that, if adopted, would convert an ad hoc emergency response into a standing policy framework. Left unaddressed, Verdant projects cumulative heatwave losses reaching £25bn by the end of 2030.

That is the throughline connecting the wildfires, the drought and the balance sheet: each Cobra meeting treats the current heat spike as a discrete event, while the underlying pattern — repeated, escalating, increasingly costly — behaves like a structural feature of the UK economy rather than a one-off shock. The test of Wednesday's meeting will not be whether it happened, but whether it produces the kind of standing measures, on fire service resourcing, water infrastructure or workplace heat rules, that a second annual Cobra convening this year suggests are overdue. The next marker is the Environment Agency's drought status update, expected within weeks, and any formal government response to Verdant's policy recommendations.

councils-vape-betting-powers.headline: Councils win new powers to block vape shops and betting parlours
councils-vape-betting-powers.body_md:
Walk down most British high streets these days and the pattern repeats: a shuttered bank, a charity shop, then — improbably often — a vape shop or a bookmaker's, sometimes two of each within a hundred yards. Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants councils to be able to say no to the next one.

On Tuesday, Burnham unveiled reforms that scrap the 'aim to permit' rule in the Gambling Act 2005, which has effectively forced local authorities to wave through new betting shops and 24-hour adult gaming centres as long as licensing boxes were ticked. In its place: standard planning permission, meaning councils can reject an application on the same grounds they'd use to block, say, an unwanted takeaway. Vape shops — previously able to open with no planning oversight at all — will be brought into the same regime, with the formal definition of a vape retailer tightened so operators can't dodge the rules by rebranding as a 'convenience store'.

> "High streets are the beating heart of local communities, but for too long Westminster has stood by" while decline set in, Burnham said.

The irony is not lost on Westminster-watchers: the 'aim to permit' rule dates to Tony Blair's 2005 liberalisation of gambling law, in a government Burnham himself served under as a minister. As Greater Manchester mayor, he was among nearly 300 politicians and campaigners who wrote to Number 10 in January calling for the rule's abolition — a campaign that has now become government policy from the top.

![William Hill betting shop on a UK high street](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/88/William_Hill_-_Lower_Town_Street_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1779021.jpg)

## The crime angle

The timing traces back to roughly eighteen months of BBC investigations linking a slice of high-street businesses — vape shops, mini-marts, some barbershops and nail salons — to organised crime: illegal cigarette and vape sales, drug dealing, immigration offences, shell companies fronting shopfronts, and in the West Midlands, evidence of premises used for child sexual exploitation. Reporters worked alongside National Crime Agency raids and, in one case, traced a tunnel supplying illegal cigarettes to shops in Hull.

Alongside the planning changes, the package extends closure orders against premises suspected of criminal links from six months to twelve, giving police and councils more time to build a case — examining ownership, financing and supply chains — without a shop reopening mid-investigation.

## The numbers behind the decline

Burnham's team is citing a stark trade-off on the high street ledger: Britain has lost nearly 1,800 pubs and bars since 2016, even as vape and tobacco shop numbers rose to roughly 2,200 over the same stretch. Betting shops have moved the other way — down by more than a third since 2019, a fall the Betting & Gaming Council put at close to 3,000 closures and 15,000 jobs, largely a product of 2019 stake limits on fixed-odds terminals and the shift to online wagering. The government's bet, so to speak, is that fewer new gambling and vape outlets will free up units for the pubs, services and community spaces that survey after survey says residents actually want back.

The Vape Trade Association's response was notably unsentimental about the rogue end of its own sector: "Rogue vape traders on the high street have been a blight on the legitimate sector." The Betting & Gaming Council, for its part, mostly stuck to restating the scale of the industry's contraction rather than contesting the reform outright.

## What it means for markets

Direct trading relevance is thin. Listed bookmakers have already pivoted most of their growth to online and app-based channels, and the betting-shop estate has been shrinking on its own for years regardless of planning law — this mainly raises the bar for reopening or relocating shops, rather than threatening existing high-street footprints. Vape retail is dominated by independents and small chains with little public-market exposure. The more relevant reader here is a local authority finance officer or a high-street landlord than a portfolio manager, though gaming-sector equities with UK expansion plans in adult gaming centres may want to note the added friction.

A fast-tracked six-week consultation is expected to open shortly, with ministers targeting the start of 2027 for the new rules to take effect. Watch for how many councils move quickly once the powers land, and whether landlords start marketing vacant units differently in anticipation.

uk-grown-cocoa-chocolate.headline: All-British chocolate bar made using Reading-grown cocoa unveiled
uk-grown-cocoa-chocolate.body_md:
A cocoa pod does not, by any reasonable expectation, belong in Berkshire. The tree that produces it, Theobroma cacao, wants year-round heat above 20C, thick humidity and shelter from wind — the climate of the West African rainforest belt, not the Thames Valley. Yet researchers working with the University of Reading's cocoa programme have grown cocoa pods to full ripeness in a greenhouse near the town and turned the beans inside them into a chocolate bar, understood to be the first made entirely from cocoa cultivated on British soil.

> **In one sentence:** UK researchers have grown cocoa to maturity in a Reading greenhouse and turned it into what is thought to be Britain's first domestically-grown chocolate bar.

It is a novelty, and everyone involved would concede as much — a heated greenhouse is not a cocoa plantation, and nobody is proposing that Somerset take on Côte d'Ivoire. But the proof of concept lands at a pointed moment for an industry watching its main growing regions come under sustained strain.

![Cacao pods on the tree](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/21/Cacao_pods.jpg)

## A greenhouse built for quarantine, not chocolate bars

The cocoa work behind the bar traces back to the International Cocoa Quarantine Centre, a facility the University of Reading has run since 1985 in Arborfield, on the edge of Reading. Its 1,000 square metre greenhouse is kept at a tropical 23C and holds several hundred cocoa varieties, sourced mainly from genebanks in Trinidad and Costa Rica. The centre's actual job is unglamorous but consequential: it screens roughly 98% of all cocoa plant material moved internationally for breeding programmes, holding cuttings in quarantine for two years and checking them for disease before they are grafted and shipped onward — because Britain, unlike the tropics, has none of the pests or pathogens that plague cocoa where it is normally grown.

Dr Andrew Daymond, who oversees the centre, has spent years studying how cocoa responds to heat, drought and rising CO2 rather than trying to make it fruit as a crop in its own right. Getting pods to ripen and yield beans fit for a chocolate bar was, by the researchers' own account, more demonstration than agronomy — a way of showing that cocoa's biology is more flexible than its geography suggests, given enough artificial tropics.

## Why the timing matters

Cocoa production is heavily concentrated: Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana together supply roughly 60% of the world's beans. Both have had brutal few years. Unusually heavy rains in December 2023 triggered outbreaks of black pod disease, followed by drought that hammered yields further. Cocoa swollen shoot virus has since spread across an estimated 590,000 hectares of Ghana's 1.38m hectares of plantation — trees typically die within three to four years of infection, and the only real remedy is felling them. Futures prices, which spent most of the 2010s below $3,000 a tonne, spiked past $12,000 in 2024 and were still trading above $5,700 in July 2026, with forecasters flagging an 82% chance of El Niño conditions returning through the rest of the year.

Against that backdrop, a UK-grown chocolate bar reads less as whimsy and more as a data point in a wider argument about whether cocoa supply chains can adapt to a warmer, wetter, more disease-prone world — through breeding hardier varieties, shifting cultivation zones, or, per a separate and unrelated track of research, growing cocoa butter from cultured cells in a bioreactor rather than a field at all. Reading's greenhouse experiment sits closer to the first camp: not replacing tropical cultivation, but using controlled environments to understand what cocoa needs and how far its tolerances can be pushed.

## What it doesn't solve

None of this scales. Heating and lighting a greenhouse to tropical specification is expensive, and Britain will not be exporting beans. The value of the exercise is scientific rather than commercial: a working proof that cocoa's genetics can tolerate cultivation well outside its native range, which feeds directly into breeding programmes trying to develop varieties more resistant to the droughts and diseases now ravaging West African farms. Reading's germplasm bank already exists for exactly that purpose.

The next marker to watch is less a laboratory demonstration than a market one — how the 2026/27 West African harvest holds up through the remainder of the El Niño risk window, and whether swollen shoot virus containment in Ghana's Western North region slows the disease's spread before it reaches more of the country's 1.38m hectares under cultivation.
